stem: A 12-year-old boy has a closed femoral fracture after a quadbike rollover. He is haemodynamically stable but has a markedly swollen thigh and weaker distal pulses, suggesting bleeding into the thigh and threatened limb perfusion. Orthopaedics are delayed. Which single management step is most likely to provide pain relief, help control haemorrhage, and improve circulation at this stage?
explanation: Immobilisation/splintage of a femoral fracture reduces pain, limits ongoing bleeding into the thigh, and can improve limb perfusion by stabilising the fracture ends. It is the key immediate management step while awaiting definitive orthopaedic care.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Trauma 2 - Pain

rationale: Closed femoral fractures can hide significant blood loss in the thigh; immobilisation is the immediate step that addresses pain, haemorrhage, and circulation together.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: stabilises the fracture, reduces pain, and helps limit haemorrhage and further soft tissue injury.
optionExplanations.B: May provide analgesia, but does not control fracture bleeding or improve limb stability.
optionExplanations.C: Useful for external bleeding, but not for a closed femoral fracture bleeding into the thigh.
optionExplanations.D: May reduce distress, but has no effect on haemorrhage or fracture stability.
optionExplanations.E: Provides analgesia, but does not stabilise the fracture or address ongoing bleeding.

source.quizTitle: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Trauma 2 - Pain
source.questionTextHtml:
Brayden remains in pain and discomfort, although better after analgaesia. His airway and breathing appear stable. Circulatory assessment confirms normal heart rate and blood pressure, chest clear, abdomen and pelvis clear. Brayden has an obviously shortened, externally rotated right leg, with a tender, solid, markedly swollen right thigh. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable but weaker on comparison to the contralateral limb.

You suspect Brayden suffered a femoral fracture and is bleeding into the thigh; it appears to be a closed injury. There do not appear to be any life-threatening injuries on initial assessment, but a potentially limb-threatening one. The trauma radiographer performs a top-down shoot through of the leg, in addition to the trauma series. The accompanying image shows an example of such an x-ray, although not of a 12 year old (Reference: UpToDate www.uptodate.com). You contact the on-call orthopaedic team, who are tied up in theatre, but will attend as soon as possible.

Which of the following management options at this stage will provide pain relief, control of haemorrhage and improvement of circulation? Please note more than one answer may be correct.

Clinical scenario 1 - Braydon

The following six questions refer to Brayden’s clinical scenario.

Teaching/learning points:

Pain relief

Primary survey in context of distracting injury

Paramedics arrive in the emergency department with Brayden, a 12 year old boy. They were called to attend after Brayden lost control of his quadbike (recreational vehicles) while riding around in a field. He was found on his back, alert and screaming in pain. Eyewitnesses stated he had been travelling at approximately 40kph when he lost control at a bend and the quadbike rolled.

Brayden has an obvious deformity to his right lower limb. He was wearing a helmet, which was removed at the scene. He is transported to ED on a spinal board with hard collar in situ. Vital signs are Resp rate 28/min, Sats 100% in air, Heart rate 100bpm, BP 118/65. He has a grossly deformed right leg, with a firm, swollen thigh and he is screaming in pain.
